target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society because it improves convenience, work/learning, accessibility, and safety.
objection: Even when AI is helpful, it creates major harms that outweigh the benefits: it threatens economic well-being by displacing workers and concentrating power, undermines critical thinking by encouraging shallow answer-taking, can worsen racism by scaling biased patterns, and poses serious privacy risks through large-scale data collection and profiling.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s harms are not inevitable because they can be managed by responsible policy and design.
objection: In practice, the harms are structurally more likely than the safeguards because firms have incentives to use AI for cost reduction, users tend to take the easiest path and bypass learning, fairness fixes cannot eliminate bias entirely, and privacy-preserving techniques do not stop the broader data-collection and profiling pressures of AI ecosystems.

target: AG1’s argument that mandatory audits, documentation, liability, and human review can make AI safe enough to be socially beneficial.
objection: Those governance tools can become compliance theater: audits can miss black-box failures or be gamed, model updates outpace pre-deployment checks, regulators may lack capacity to enforce rules, and companies can race to deploy first and fix later, so safeguards cannot reliably keep up with real-world deployment incentives.

target: AG1’s proposal to use risk-tiered deployment, ongoing monitoring, red-teaming, and selective restrictions to contain AI harms.
objection: Harm does not stay confined to intended low-risk uses because models, data, and capabilities spill over across domains; firms controlling frontier AI gain leverage over workers and smaller institutions; and emergent harms can appear faster than continuous monitoring can catch them.

target: AG1’s claim that purpose limitation, data governance, competition policy, and phased rollouts can prevent spillover and power concentration.
objection: AI can still erode autonomy and democratic accountability by making outcomes opaque and hard to contest, creating loss of agency, chilling effects from surveillance/profiling, and manipulation at scale through targeted content that governance cannot easily contain.

target: AG1’s claim that due-process safeguards, explanations, logging, and opt-outs can make AI decisions contestable and accountable.
objection: AI can scale synthetic content that people cannot reliably verify, enabling deepfake fraud, scams, information flooding, and an arms race in detection and verification that weakens critical thinking and public deliberation.

target: AG1’s claim that non-AI fallback pathways, meaningful appeals, and reduced vendor lock-in can prevent AI from becoming a default gatekeeper.
objection: Those fixes often fail in practice because fallback paths can be nominal, appeals require resources that many people lack, and the entity deploying AI controls the alternatives, so AI still restructures power and undermines autonomy even when procedures exist on paper.

target: AG1’s claim that implementation failures can be fixed with stronger design constraints, privacy minimization, and better appeal systems.
objection: These solutions often create new problems: non-AI pathways can still be driven by AI behind the scenes, meaningful appeals require collecting and retaining more personal data and logs, and under-resourced institutions may only offer rubber-stamp contestability, worsening privacy and inequality.

target: AG1’s argument that lower-risk, narrower AI can provide the same upsides without major harms.
objection: Society can obtain many of the claimed benefits through lower-risk alternatives such as narrowly scoped tools, human tutoring, established assistive technologies, and direct investment in staff and training, so broad AI deployment is not uniquely necessary and still brings scalable harms.

target: AG1’s claim that avoiding powerful general AI is enough, because narrow AI can still be safely regulated by use case and capability.
objection: Even narrow, data-driven automation can still cause bias, privacy leakage, opaque decisions, and fraud; vendors can blur use-case boundaries; harms such as autonomy loss and critical-thinking degradation are hard to measure in advance; and systems change over time, making capability-based governance unreliable.

target: AG1’s claim that reversible, metric-based pilots and stop/go controls can justify AI deployment.
objection: Many harms are irreversible or externalized: personal data can be copied or embedded into models and cannot be fully rolled back, misinformation and fraud can spread before metrics stabilize, long-term displacement and learning harms are under-measured, and pilots can create dependencies that make later reversal difficult.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be used to strengthen oversight faster than deployment, through monitoring, audits, provenance systems, and AI-assisted appeals.
objection: Using AI for governance can itself worsen the problems it is meant to solve because it expands surveillance and data collection, relies on opaque tools that are hard to audit, and concentrates power in the same vendors that built the original systems.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-minimized oversight and independent auditing can avoid surveillance harms.
objection: That concern is a design choice, not an unavoidable consequence; properly engineered AI governance can use aggregated or anonymized metrics, standardized independent audits, and privacy-preserving oversight while still delivering concrete safety benefits such as fewer workplace injuries.

target: AG1’s claim that feedback loops can be broken through monitoring, causal testing, and corrective interventions.
objection: AI systems create self-reinforcing feedback loops, especially for racial bias, because their outputs affect real-world decisions that become the next round of training data; this compounds errors over time and across institutions in ways that standard audits and contestability do not reliably stop.

target: AG1’s claim that ongoing outcome monitoring, counterfactual testing, and retraining can prevent biased feedback loops.
objection: AI’s dual-use security risks make net benefits unreliable because it can automate phishing and impersonation, speed up malware and exploit development, and increase the verification burden on everyone, expanding the harm surface across society.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can also strengthen security and therefore its dual-use risks do not make it net harmful.
objection: The attacker–defender asymmetry means misuse is cheaper and faster than widespread defense, defensive capacity is unevenly distributed, victims bear the costs of verification and fraud, and the result is a continuing arms race that consumes resources and harms economic well-being.
